objectives: I can give distinct differences between CISC and RISC processors and link each to a typical use
I can explain how a GPU achieves high performance and identify workloads suited to GPUs, including GPGPU uses
I can describe multicore and parallel systems and explain what limits the benefit of adding cores
I can justify a choice of processor type for a given scenario using hardware features

retrieval.q: Last week: list the four fetch-stage register transfers in order.
retrieval.a: PC copied to MAR; instruction from memory via data bus into MDR; PC incremented; MDR copied to CIR.

retrieval.q: Last week: which bus is unidirectional, and what does an n-bit width of it determine?
retrieval.a: The address bus; n bits gives 2^n directly addressable memory locations.

retrieval.q: Last week: state the difference between the MAR and the MDR.
retrieval.a: MAR holds the address of the location to access; MDR holds the data or instruction itself.

retrieval.q: Last week: why does a branch instruction reduce the benefit of pipelining?
retrieval.a: It writes a new address into the PC, so prefetched instructions in the pipeline must be flushed.

retrieval.q: Last week: in what order does the CPU check cache levels before RAM?
retrieval.a: L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM; L1 is the smallest and fastest.

keywords.def: Complex Instruction Set Computer; a large set of complex, variable-length instructions taking multiple cycles.
Reduced Instruction Set Computer; a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions aiming for one cycle each.
The complete collection of machine-code operations a particular processor can execute.
Graphics Processing Unit; thousands of small cores applying the same operation to large data blocks in parallel.
General-purpose computing on a GPU; using it for non-graphics work such as machine learning.
Applying the same operation independently to many data items at the same time.
A single chip containing two or more independent cores, each running its own FDE cycle.
Splitting a task so multiple computations are carried out simultaneously across cores or processors.
The part of a task that must run in sequence and so cannot be shared across cores.

content.heading: Instruction sets: two design philosophies
points: An instruction set is the full list of machine-code operations a CPU understands
Designers face a trade-off: many powerful instructions, or few simple ones executed very fast
CISC and RISC are the two resulting philosophies, and both are on the spec
Last week's architecture (registers, FDE, pipeline) explains why each choice has consequences

content.heading: CISC: Complex Instruction Set Computers
points: Large set of complex instructions; a single instruction can do several low-level jobs
Instructions are variable length and take multiple clock cycles
Complexity sits in the HARDWARE, so compilers do less work and machine code is compact
Needs more power and generates more heat; typical of x86 desktop and laptop processors

content.heading: RISC: Reduced Instruction Set Computers
points: Small set of simple, fixed-length instructions, each aiming to complete in one clock cycle
Complexity moves to the SOFTWARE: the compiler builds complex behaviour from many simple instructions
Fewer transistors needed, so lower power consumption and less heat
Typical of ARM processors in phones, tablets and embedded devices

content.heading: Why RISC pipelines so well
points: Pipelining works best when every stage takes the same, predictable time
Fixed-length, one-cycle RISC instructions slot cleanly into pipeline stages
Variable-length, multi-cycle CISC instructions stall stages and complicate the pipeline
Modern x86 chips even translate CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-operations internally
content.note: Exam answers need DISTINCT differences: set size, instruction length, cycles per instruction, where complexity lies.

content.heading: Choosing CISC or RISC for a scenario
points: Battery-powered or embedded device: RISC, for low power, less heat and cheap simple hardware
Desktop running legacy software: CISC (x86), for compatibility and compact code
Give the hardware justification, not just the label: instruction length, cycles, power, pipelining
The real world is blurring: Apple Silicon laptops are RISC; many servers now use ARM

content.heading: GPUs: built for data parallelism
points: A GPU contains thousands of small, simple cores; a CPU has a few powerful ones
GPU cores apply the SAME operation to large blocks of data simultaneously (data parallelism)
Perfect for graphics: the same transformation applied to millions of pixels or vertices per frame
Weak at branch-heavy, sequential, dependency-laden work — that still belongs on the CPU
content.note: Explain GPU speed with BOTH ideas: thousands of cores AND the same operation on many data items.

content.heading: GPGPU: general-purpose uses of GPUs
points: GPGPU means using a GPU for non-graphics computation
Machine learning and neural-network training: the same weight calculations across huge data sets
Scientific modelling, e.g. weather simulation over a grid of cells
Image and video processing, and cryptocurrency hash calculations
Caveat: software must be specifically written to run on the GPU

content.heading: Multicore processors
points: A multicore processor has two or more independent cores on one chip
Each core runs its own FDE cycle, so different instructions execute simultaneously
Cores typically have private L1 and L2 caches but share L3 cache and main memory
The operating system schedules threads and processes across the cores

content.heading: Parallel processing and its limits
points: Parallel processing splits one task into parts computed simultaneously across cores
The serial fraction limits the benefit: steps depending on earlier results cannot be parallelised
Coordination overhead: splitting work and combining results costs time
Software must be written for multiple threads, or extra cores sit idle
If 20 percent of a task is inherently serial, the best possible speed-up is 5 times

worked_examples.title: Choosing between a multicore CPU and a GPU for a workload
steps: Scenario: apply the same brightness calculation to every one of the 2 million pixels in a photo
Step 1, identify the workload type: the same operation repeated over huge data, no branching, each pixel independent — highly data-parallel
Step 2, match to hardware: a GPU's thousands of small cores process many pixels simultaneously; a CPU's few powerful cores suit sequential, branch-heavy work
Step 3, add the caveat: the software must be written to use the GPU; a branchy task like a chess engine would suit the CPU instead
Step 4, conclude: for this uniform, massively parallel task the GPU maximises throughput, so it is the better choice

worked_examples.title: Counting cycles: why RISC pipelines beat serial execution
steps: A RISC processor runs 6 fixed-length instructions through a 3-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute)
Without pipelining: 6 instructions x 3 cycles = 18 cycles
With pipelining: the first instruction completes at cycle 3, then one completes every cycle: total = 6 + 3 - 1 = 8 cycles
Why CISC struggles: variable-length, multi-cycle instructions make the stages uneven, causing stalls that reduce this gain

worked_examples.title: The serial-fraction limit on multicore speed-up
steps: A task takes 100 seconds on one core; 80 seconds of it is parallelisable, 20 seconds is inherently serial
With 4 cores, the parallel part takes 80 / 4 = 20 seconds; total = 20 + 20 = 40 seconds, i.e. 2.5 times faster
With 80 cores, the parallel part takes 80 / 80 = 1 second; total = 20 + 1 = 21 seconds
Even with unlimited cores the total can never drop below the 20-second serial part
So the maximum possible speed-up is 100 / 20 = 5 times — the serial fraction caps the benefit

activities.title: RISC or CISC? Decision Continuum
instructions: Mark an imaginary line across the room: one wall is definitely RISC, the other definitely CISC
Read a scenario; students stand along the line — no fence-sitting in the exact middle without a spoken reason

Scenarios: a fitness tracker running two weeks on a coin cell; a desktop workstation running legacy x86 software; a drone flight controller; a data-centre server prioritising performance per watt; the student's own laptop
Interview outliers and clusters: what feature of the scenario put you there?
After each scenario one student must give the hardware justification (instruction length, cycles per instruction, power, pipelining) before moving on
Expected: tracker RISC; legacy desktop CISC; drone RISC; server defensibly RISC (ARM); laptop genuinely mixed — reward students who ask which laptop
activities.stretch: Modern x86 chips translate CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-ops internally — does the distinction still matter? Defend a position.

activities.title: CPU or GPU? Corner Sort
instructions: Label two corners CPU and GPU, plus a third spot labelled It Depends
Read a workload; students walk to a corner within five seconds, then justify on request

Workloads: training a neural network; applying a filter to every pixel of a photo; running the OS scheduler; a chess engine searching deep branching game trees; mining cryptocurrency hashes; simulating weather across a grid; parsing source code
Expected: GPU for neural network, pixel filter, hashing, weather grid (same operation, huge data); CPU for scheduler, chess search, parsing (sequential, branchy, dependent)
Finish: every student writes the rule of thumb in one sentence on a whiteboard
activities.stretch: If 20 percent of a task is inherently serial, what is the best possible speed-up however many cores you add? (5 times.)

activities.title: Analogy Autopsy: 1,000 Pupils vs 4 Professors
instructions: Display the analogy: a GPU is 1,000 primary-school pupils each doing one simple sum; a CPU is 4 professors solving hard problems one after another
Think (1 minute): individually list what the analogy gets right
Pair (2 minutes): find at least two places it breaks down
Share: harvest onto a two-column board, Holds Up versus Breaks Down

Key breakdowns to surface: GPU cores work in lockstep on the same instruction while pupils could each freelance a different sum; no coordination or memory-bandwidth cost is shown; the professors (CPU cores) also work in parallel with each other
Pairs propose a one-word patch to the analogy that fixes one flaw
activities.stretch: Write a better original analogy for GPGPU or multicore and give it to a partner for autopsy.

practice.q: Describe three differences between RISC and CISC processors. [3]
practice.a: RISC has a small set of simple instructions whereas CISC has a large set of complex instructions (1); RISC instructions are fixed length and aim to complete in one clock cycle whereas CISC instructions are variable length and take multiple cycles (1); in RISC the complexity is handled by the compiler/software whereas in CISC it is built into the hardware (1). Also credit: RISC uses less power / pipelines more easily.

practice.q: A smartwatch manufacturer must choose between a RISC and a CISC processor. Explain why RISC is likely to be more suitable. [3]
practice.a: RISC processors use simpler circuitry with fewer transistors so they consume less power (1), extending battery life and producing less heat inside a small sealed case (1); the simple fixed-length instructions pipeline efficiently, giving sufficient performance for the watch's limited tasks (1).

practice.q: Explain how the design of a GPU makes it well suited to rendering 3D graphics. [3]
practice.a: A GPU contains thousands of small cores (1) that apply the same operation to large blocks of data in parallel (1); rendering repeats the same calculation for millions of independent pixels/vertices, so many can be processed simultaneously (1).

practice.q: State what is meant by GPGPU and give two examples of non-graphics uses of a GPU. [3]
practice.a: GPGPU is using a GPU for general-purpose, non-graphics computation (1); examples for the other two marks: training machine-learning/neural networks; scientific simulations such as weather modelling; large-scale image or video processing; cryptocurrency hash calculations.

practice.q: Define the terms multicore processor and parallel processing. [2]
practice.a: A multicore processor is a single chip containing two or more independent cores, each able to run its own fetch-decode-execute cycle (1); parallel processing is splitting a task so multiple computations are carried out simultaneously across cores or processors (1).

practice.q: A video-editing program renders a film in 100 seconds on one core; 80 seconds of the work can be shared perfectly across cores and 20 seconds cannot. Calculate the render time on 4 cores. [2]
practice.a: Parallel part: 80 / 4 = 20 seconds (1); total = 20 serial + 20 parallel = 40 seconds (1).

practice.q: Explain two reasons why doubling the number of cores may not halve a program's run time. [4]
practice.a: Part of the task may be inherently serial because each step depends on the previous result, so it cannot be split across cores (1), and this serial fraction sets a floor on the run time (1). The software must also be written to use multiple threads, otherwise extra cores sit idle (1), and dividing work then combining results adds coordination overhead (1).

practice.q: A research lab must apply the same statistical operation to billions of independent sensor readings. Discuss whether a multicore CPU or a GPU is more appropriate. [4]
practice.a: The workload applies the same operation to a huge number of independent data items, so it is data-parallel (1); a GPU's thousands of cores can process many readings simultaneously, giving far higher throughput than a CPU's few cores (1); however the software must be written specifically for the GPU (1); as there is little branching or dependency, the GPU is the more appropriate choice, with the CPU handling sequential control work (1).

misconceptions: Students often think RISC means weaker or slower, but simple one-cycle instructions plus easy pipelining can give equal or better performance per watt.
Students often think a GPU is just a faster CPU, but its thousands of cores apply the same operation in lockstep — it only wins on data-parallel work.
Students often think more cores always means proportionally faster, but the serial fraction, data dependencies and unthreaded software cap the speed-up.
Students often give one RISC/CISC difference reworded several times; examiners want distinct points — set size, instruction length, cycles, where complexity lies.
Students often think GPUs are only for graphics, but GPGPU covers machine learning, simulation and hashing.
exam_link: Command words: Define/State (1-2 marks on terms), Describe (RISC vs CISC differences, 3 marks), Explain (why a processor suits a device, 3-4 marks), Discuss (processor choice for a scenario, up to 9-mark levels of response).
RISC vs CISC comparison questions penalise repeated points reworded — plan three genuinely distinct differences before writing.
Example stem: 'A company is developing a battery-powered drone. Discuss the suitability of RISC and CISC processors for this product.' — link every hardware feature to the scenario.
GPU questions expect the two-part mechanism (many cores AND same operation on much data) plus the software-support caveat for full marks.
task: For each of these four devices, choose CISC, RISC, GPU-assisted or multicore-focused and justify with at least two hardware features linked to the device's needs: a hearing aid, a 3D-rendering workstation, a supermarket checkout, and a machine-learning research server.
challenge: A task takes 200 seconds on one core; 150 seconds of it parallelises perfectly. Calculate the run times on 2, 5 and 50 cores (125 s, 80 s, 53 s) and the theoretical minimum (50 s), then write three sentences explaining what this tells a buyer comparing an 8-core CPU with a 64-core CPU.

exit_ticket.q: Give two distinct differences between RISC and CISC.
exit_ticket.a: Any two of: small simple set vs large complex set; fixed-length one-cycle vs variable-length multi-cycle instructions; complexity in compiler/software vs in hardware; lower vs higher power.

exit_ticket.q: What TWO ideas must you combine to explain why a GPU is fast?
exit_ticket.a: It has thousands of cores, and it applies the same operation to many data items in parallel.

exit_ticket.q: Name two things that limit the benefit of adding more cores.
exit_ticket.a: Any two of: the serial fraction/data dependencies, software not written for multiple threads, coordination overhead.
